Listen to this article Share The Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC) is moving to establish a cost-based pricing framework for value-added services (VAS) as concerns over pricing disparities, revenue-sharing arrangements and billing transparency expose structural weaknesses in Nigeria’s telecommunications value chain. Advertisement Advertisement This is even as the Commission has commissioned a study to determine the actual cost of providing VAS, a market involving mobile network operators, aggregators, service providers and content developers, which has operated without a common cost benchmark for pricing and revenue-sharing arrangements. The exercise could provide the regulatory basis for reviewing how revenues are distributed among players, particularly where differences in commercial agreements and operating costs influence the margins earned by participants. Aminu Maida, executive vice-chairman of the NCC, disclosed this on Thursday at the Stakeholders’ Consultative Forum on the Cost Determination of Value-Added Services in the Nigerian Telecommunications Industry in Lagos. Maida, who was represented by Omotayo Mohammed, head of competition and tariff unit at the Commission, said the study would provide an evidence-based understanding of costs across the VAS value chain and help identify inefficiencies and structural imbalances. “Our objective is not to predetermine pricing outcomes, but to establish a credible and transparent cost basis that supports fair competition, efficient cost recovery, continued investment, innovation and consumer welfare,” he said. Advertisement The proposed benchmark comes against the backdrop of a market where mobile network operators, aggregators and content developers negotiate commercial arrangements without a common reference for determining the costs and appropriate revenue shares associated with delivering services. Olusegun Ekundayo, project director at Skyquest Concept Projects Ltd., the consultant handling the study, said Nigeria currently lacked a cost-based regulatory benchmark for VAS pricing and revenue-sharing arrangements. Advertisement He noted that the absence of a common cost reference had contributed to variations in prices, service quality and margins across the value chain. For content developers and smaller service providers, the absence of a transparent cost framework raises questions about how much value they retain from services delivered through network operators and aggregators. For operators and aggregators, it also creates differences in how commercial arrangements are structured and costs recovered. Advertisement Advertisement The NCC’s intervention therefore goes beyond establishing service prices. It could provide a common basis for assessing whether existing revenue-sharing arrangements adequately reflect the investments, infrastructure and services contributed by different participants. The commission, however, has not announced any decision to impose uniform prices or alter existing revenue-sharing agreements. Rather, it says the findings will guide future regulatory decisions. The study will examine the sector between 2017 and 2025, covering traditional services such as Short Message Service (SMS), Unstructured Supplementary Service Data (USSD), Interactive Voice Response (IVR) and web-based services. It will also assess emerging segments, including artificial intelligence, fifth-generation (5G) networks, Internet of Things (IoT), Over-the-Top (OTT) services and technology providers offering cloud and application services. Read also: Nigeria secures seat on ITU Council as Africa wins 13 positions in global telecoms governance The expanded scope reflects the changing economics of value-added services, which increasingly extend beyond conventional mobile subscriptions into digital content, financial applications, cloud-based solutions and connected devices. Ekundayo cited a projected global VAS market value of $1.07 trillion in his presentation, highlighting the growing economic significance of the segment. Beyond commercial disputes, consumer protection remains another major concern driving the regulatory exercise. The NCC identified billing transparency, consumer consent, unsolicited subscriptions and unauthorised deductions as issues requiring attention. These concerns have persisted despite regulatory interventions intended to protect subscribers from being enrolled in services without their knowledge or charged for subscriptions they did not authorise. The commission introduced its VAS Aggregator Framework in 2017 and amended it in 2018 to improve connections between content providers and network operators, address market-access concerns and strengthen revenue-sharing arrangements. It also introduced consumer safeguards, including the Do-Not-Disturb (DND) mechanism and short codes, to improve control over unsolicited communications and subscriptions. However, the latest study suggests that improving access and consumer safeguards alone may not address the underlying cost and commercial structures governing the market. A more transparent cost framework could help the regulator distinguish between legitimate service-delivery costs, commercial margins and pricing practices that may undermine competition or consumer welfare. Maida urged industry stakeholders to cooperate with Skyquest Concept Projects by providing accurate and relevant information, warning that delayed, incomplete or inconsistent submissions could undermine the reliability of the findings. He assured participants that commercially sensitive information submitted during the exercise would remain confidential and that the consultants were contractually obligated to protect such data. The NCC also invoked Section 64 of the Nigerian Communications Act 2003, which empowers it to request relevant information and documents from licensed operators and other regulated entities. The commission expects stakeholders to provide truthful, complete and accurate responses within stipulated deadlines, appoint focal persons and notify it early of any challenges in submitting the requested information. The findings could shape the next phase of regulation in Nigeria’s VAS market, particularly as new digital services introduce more participants, complex delivery arrangements and competing claims over the value generated across the telecommunications ecosystem.
